sentences: In an age where everything moves quickly, where screens offer videos of just a few seconds, one might think that the novel is doomed.
Why spend hours on a book when there are so many faster distractions available?
And yet, people continue to read.
Every year, millions of novels are sold around the world.
This success deserves our attention.
The novel offers something rare: time.
It forces us to slow down, to follow a story, to enter the mind of a character.
Unlike an image, it doesn't show everything; it allows the reader to imagine.
Reading a novel is also about living, for a few pages, a life that is not our own.
We understand others better when we have shared, even through fiction, their doubts and joys.
The form of the book may change over time.
But the need for stories will likely never disappear.

sentences: Last month, I made a big decision: I adopted a cat.
My apartment was too quiet, too empty.
One Saturday morning, I finally went to the animal shelter.
There, there were many cats.
A volunteer guided me between the cages.
And then I saw him: a little gray cat, sitting at the back of his cage.
He wasn't moving.
He was just looking at me, with big green eyes.
He had been found in the street and he was afraid of people.
"He needs someone patient," said the volunteer.
I chose him.
At home, I named him Gribouille.
The first week was difficult.
He was hiding under the bed all day and he hardly ate anything.
I followed the volunteer's advice.
I never forced him.
I spoke to him softly, I left his food near the bed, and I waited.
On the eighth day, a surprise: Gribouille jumped onto the couch, next to me.
I didn't move.
After ten minutes, he closed his eyes and he purred.
A small victory that made me very happy.
Today, a month later, Gribouille sleeps on my bed and he waits for me behind the door in the evening.
When I come home from work, he runs towards me meowing.
My apartment is no longer quiet and empty.
It is alive.
Thank you, Gribouille.

sentences: Coffee has a tumultuous medical history.
In the 1980s, it was blamed for all sorts of ailments: bad for the heart, bad for the stomach, bad for the nerves.
Then the tide turned, and articles began to praise its almost miraculous benefits.
So, is it poison or a remedy?
As often happens with health matters, the truth is less dramatic and more interesting.
What does science say today?
The large studies conducted on hundreds of thousands of people are rather reassuring.
Moderate consumption — two to four cups a day — does not increase heart risks for most people.
Some research even suggests protective effects against several diseases.
However, caution is warranted: these studies show statistical links, not absolute proof.
Coffee drinkers may have other habits that explain part of the results.
What we understand well, however, is the mechanism of caffeine.
In our brain, a substance called adenosine accumulates throughout the day and gradually makes us want to sleep.
Caffeine resembles this molecule and takes its place, like someone sitting in your chair.
As a result, the signal of fatigue no longer gets through.
We are not less tired — we simply don't feel it anymore.
The nuance is important.
This is also why evening coffee is a bad idea for many people.
Caffeine stays in the body for a long time: half of it is still there five or six hours after the cup.
An espresso at five o'clock still works against your sleep at ten o'clock.
And poor sleep makes you tired, and fatigue leads you to drink more coffee the next day.
The classic vicious circle.
Finally, it should be noted that we are very unequal when it comes to caffeine.
Some break it down quickly and sleep very well after a late coffee; others still feel the effects of a cup drunk at noon.
This difference is largely genetic.
The only true expert on your coffee is therefore your own body.
In summary: if you love coffee, drink it without guilt, preferably before mid-afternoon, and without exceeding what suits you.
Beware of headlines, in either direction.
And remember that the best coffee is the one you take the time to savor — ideally with someone.

sentences: When we say the word 'nature', our imagination immediately soars far away: tropical forests, African savannas, big cats, birds in improbable colors.
That nature, spectacular and distant, captures our attention and our worries.
In doing so, we forget another nature, infinitely closer and just as threatened: the one that teems in our gardens, parks, streets, right at our feet.
Biodiversity is not just an issue of the tropics; it also plays out right at our doorstep, and there, we can take action.
For a simple garden, a bank, an old wall harbors a world of unsuspected richness.
Dozens of species of insects, birds, hedgehogs, bats, frogs, not to mention countless plants and soil microorganisms: it's a whole living fabric, each thread depending on the others.
Bees and butterflies pollinate the flowers, which our fruits depend on; birds and bats regulate the insects; worms and fungi create the very soil.
This ordinary biodiversity, invisible from being so familiar, provides services whose importance we only realize when they are lacking.
But they are starting to be lacking.
The decline is spectacular, including — and this is the most alarming part — in our temperate regions and even in cities.
Studies on insects are staggering: in certain areas of Europe, their mass has dropped by more than three-quarters in just a few decades.
Many remember windshields covered in mosquitoes after a summer drive; younger generations no longer know this phenomenon, not by luck, but because the insects have disappeared.
The causes are piling up: chemicals, the disappearance of hedges and meadows, soil artificialization, nighttime lighting that disorients and exhausts nocturnal species.
This observation could be overwhelming.
However, it has an encouraging counterpart, specific to this local biodiversity: everyone can act on it, concretely, at their own scale.
Unlike the Amazon rainforest, where an individual can do almost nothing, the garden, balcony, and yard offer immediate grounds for action.
Let a patch of grass grow freely instead of mowing it down.
Give up pesticides.
Plant local species and nectar-rich flowers.
Install a water point, a pile of wood, a shelter.
Turn off unnecessary lights at night.
These tiny gestures, multiplied by millions of gardens, create a network of refuges that can make a real difference.
It would be naive to believe that these individual initiatives alone will suffice, without ambitious policies or profound agricultural changes; it would be just as wrong to deem them trivial.
They have a double virtue: a concrete effect on local life, and an effect on ourselves.
For by welcoming wildlife into our homes, we relearn to look at it, to become attached to it, to feel responsible for it.
We stop viewing nature as a distant backdrop to be preserved 'over there' and instead recognize it as a daily presence beside us.
Protecting biodiversity is therefore not just the concern of large protected areas and international summits.
It is also, and perhaps primarily, a matter of everyday life, starting in a patch of lawn left in peace.

"Forty-two," replies the farmer.
My daughter touches a cow.
Its skin is warm.
The cow doesn't move.
Next, we are going to see the chickens.
They run everywhere and make noise.
The farmer shows a small wooden house.
Inside, there are eggs.
They are still warm!

The farmer laughs.

It is huge and pink.
It makes a terrible noise: "OINK!"
The children are a little scared, then they laugh.
In the end, we buy cheese and eggs.

When they left, I did the dishes and tidied up a bit.

I was a little sad: the weekend was over.
But I was rested.

sentences: We have more means of communication than any previous generation.
Messages, photos, free video calls to the other side of the world: everything is technically possible.
And yet, long-distance friendships continue to fade away, often without arguments and without any decision.
This paradox is partly explained by the nature of these tools.
They are excellent for brief and frequent contact: a photo, a reaction, a three-word message.
They are much less suited to what really builds a relationship, namely a long conversation without a specific goal.
However, we easily confuse the two.
Seeing someone's posts regularly gives the impression of keeping in touch.
In reality, we follow their life without ever talking to them.
The feeling of closeness increases while the relationship, on the other hand, deteriorates.
What works, according to those who maintain long-distance friendships over the years, comes down to two things.
The first is the chosen regularity.
A fixed appointment — the first Sunday of the month, a thirty-minute call — holds up much better than the good intention of calling each other 'soon.'
Without a date, time passes and awkwardness sets in.
The second is accepting that the relationship changes form.
A long-distance friendship cannot be what it was when we saw each other every week.
Wanting to find exactly the same thing mostly leads to disappointment.
I have a friend in Canada for six years.
We talk every other Sunday morning.
It's not much.
But it's written in both our calendars, and that's probably why it lasts.

sentences: We consume information all day long without asking how it was made.
Yet this process explains a large part of what surprises or annoys us.
It all starts with a selection.
Every day, there are infinitely more events than a newspaper can cover.
We have to choose, and this choice follows fairly consistent criteria: novelty, proximity, the number of people involved, and the spectacular or unusual nature.
This last criterion explains a well-known bias.
A plane crash is news; thousands of planes landing normally are not.
As a result, we overestimate rare and spectacular risks, while underestimating frequent and mundane risks.
Next comes the collection.
The journalist rarely has direct access: they rely on sources — press releases, experts, witnesses, agency dispatches.
Each source has its own interests, which is not necessarily a problem, as long as it is known.
Then comes writing and editing.
The text is shortened, structured, and prioritized.
An article starts with the essentials, because many readers will only read the beginning.
Finally, the title.
This is the most misleading step, because it is almost never written by the article's author, and it must grab attention.
A title can therefore be more categorical than the text it introduces.
Hence a very concrete piece of advice: never share an article that you have only read the title of.
Studies show that this happens extremely often.
Reading the article takes two minutes.
That is enough to avoid half of the misunderstandings.

sentences: The wolf had disappeared from France in the 1930s, eliminated by hunting.
It reappeared in 1992, in the Mercantour Park, having come from Italy on its own.
This point is important: the wolf was not reintroduced.
It returned alone, thanks to reforestation and the protection it receives at the European level.
Since then, its population has grown and spread to many departments.
The debate it generates is intense, and both positions are based on real arguments.

On the protection side, it is emphasized that the wolf is a protected species, that it plays a role in regulating herbivore populations, and that its return indicates an improvement in natural environments.
On the farmers' side, the difficulty is real.
Attacks on herds number in the thousands each year.
Beyond the compensated losses, farmers describe an additional workload and constant tension: monitoring, grouping, maintaining fences, and poor sleep.
It must be recognized that protecting herds in difficult grazing areas is not always possible.
Protection dogs work well, but they pose other problems, especially with hikers.
Current policies combine species protection, compensation, support for protective measures, and regulated culling of a limited number of individuals.
This solution does not fully satisfy anyone, which may be inevitable.
The return of the wolf actually raises a broader question: how far are we willing to share territory with a wild fauna that we had eliminated?

sentences: There is a considerable amount of work that does not appear in any economic statistics: domestic tasks, childcare, and caring for elderly relatives, as well as the daily organization of a household.
This work is unpaid, so it is not counted.
Nevertheless, it is essential: without it, no professional activity would be possible.
Surveys on time use regularly measure its distribution.
They show a constant reality, even though the gap is slowly narrowing: women do the largest share, even when both partners work full-time.
To this burden is added an even less visible dimension, which researchers call mental load.
It is not just about performing a task, but about thinking about it: knowing that you need to make a dentist appointment, that the shoes are too small, that a gift is needed for Saturday.
This anticipatory load is difficult to share because it is invisible as long as it is well managed.
One only notices its existence when it stops.
The consequences are concrete: it is mostly women who reduce their working hours or interrupt their careers, which then impacts salaries and pensions.
Solutions exist at several levels: accessible childcare services, truly shared parental leave, and recognition of the caregiver status.
But part of it is played out within households, in an explicitly discussed distribution.
Couples who succeed in this often describe the same method.
They did not share the tasks.

sentences: There is such a constant regularity that it becomes a rule: a renovation costs more and takes longer than expected.
It's not a question of incompetence.
The phenomenon has structural causes.
The first is the invisible.
In an old house, you only discover the true condition of the walls, floors, and systems by opening them up.
A quote established before the work is therefore partially based on assumptions, and unpleasant surprises are common: dampness, damaged framework, non-compliant electrical systems.
The second is the sequence of decisions.
Redoing the electrical work requires opening the walls; since the walls are open, it becomes absurd not to insulate; insulation changes the thickness, and therefore the carpentry.
Each decision leads to another, and the project expands without any step being unreasonable.
The third is the order of the work.
Many homeowners start with what is visible — the kitchen, the painting — and then discover that they have to undo everything to address the roof or dampness.
The correct order is constant: first the shell and the roof, then the systems, then the insulation, and only afterwards the finishes.
People who manage best generally apply two principles.
They set aside a financial reserve of about twenty percent, considered part of the budget and not an overspend.
And they have a serious diagnosis done before buying, not after.
A friend summarized his project to me like this, two years later:
"It's not that I calculated poorly."
"It's that I didn't yet know what I was buying."

sentences: We have inherited a view of learning that associates it with a specific period of life: childhood and youth.
One would learn at school, then, once the diploma is obtained, enter the working world, with learning behind them.
This view, convenient for a long time, is now doubly outdated: due to the necessities of a rapidly changing world, and because of what we now know about how the mind works.
The first reason is practical.
In a world where knowledge, techniques, and jobs are constantly evolving, stopping learning once and for all is no longer feasible.
What we learned in our youth becomes outdated, new skills become necessary, jobs appear while others disappear.
Continuing to learn is no longer a luxury or a passion reserved for a few; it is a condition for staying relevant in a changing world.
But reducing lifelong learning to this economic necessity would mean missing the essential.
For learning throughout life is not just a constraint to endure; it is also one of the great sources of vitality in existence.
Discovering, understanding, and progressing in a new field provides deep satisfaction at any age.
The mind that continues to learn remains alive, curious, and open; the one that stops gradually closes in.
Research on the brain supports this idea.
Contrary to a persistent belief, the ability to learn does not disappear with youth.
The brain retains, until an advanced age, a remarkable ability to transform itself, create new connections, and adapt.
Learning later may sometimes require more effort, but it remains entirely possible, and this very exercise helps preserve the sharpness of the mind over the years.
However, one must overcome a few internal obstacles.
The first is the belief that one is 'too old' to learn, a belief that, by discouraging attempts, proves itself.
The second is the fear of starting over, of being a beginner, of making mistakes — this fear of error which, again, hinders learning.
Accepting to be clumsy, to not know, to progress slowly is the modest price of any new learning.
Learning throughout life is therefore not just an obligation imposed by the times; it is a way to remain fully alive.
The mind, like the body, is maintained through exercise, and the day one stops learning may be the day one begins, slowly, to age.

sentences: Here is a question that we rarely dare to ask, as it seems so naive: what is the purpose of art?
A painting does not feed anyone, a symphony does not cure any disease, and a poem has never built a house.
Measured by the standard of utility, art seems perfectly superfluous.
And yet, no human society, however poor or threatened it may be, has ever chosen to do without it.
This contradiction — the apparent uselessness of art and its stubborn universality — deserves our attention.
The answer may lie in the question itself, or rather in its presupposition.
Asking what art 'is for' judges it according to the logic of utility, that of means toward an end.
However, art precisely escapes this logic.
It serves no purpose other than itself; it is not a means, but an end.
Like love, like friendship, like contemplation, it belongs to those experiences that are valuable in themselves, not for what they might lead to.
Their 'uselessness' is not a flaw: it is a sign that they touch on something beyond mere survival.
For human beings do not settle for mere survival.

Once their vital needs are met, they experience other demands, less immediate but no less profound: to give meaning to their existence, to express what they feel, to understand their condition, to experience beauty.
Art responds to these demands.
It expresses what ordinary language cannot convey, gives form to confused emotions, and allows us to share what we thought was uncommunicable.
In this sense, it serves no purpose, but it addresses everything in us that goes beyond simple necessity.
Art also has this unique power to make us experience what we will never live.
Through a novel, we inhabit another life; through a painting, we see through other eyes; through music, we feel what another person felt, centuries apart.
Art thus broadens our experience well beyond the narrow limits of our individual existence.
It connects us to others, to the dead as well as the living, in a community of emotions and meaning.
We must guard against two opposing errors here.
The first would be to disdain art as a superfluous luxury, good for times of abundance.
The second would be to turn it into a religion, to sanctify it to the point of making it intimidating, reserved for a few initiates.
Art is neither a useless ornament nor a reserved cult; it is a fundamental human need, as old as humanity itself, and accessible, in a thousand forms, to everyone.
What is the purpose of art?
None, if we understand by that a practical utility.
Everything, if we understand that a purely useful life would not be a human life.
Art does not help us to live; it is a part of what makes life worth living.

sentences: Sometimes, to discredit science, a decisive criticism is heard: it changes its mind.
What it asserted yesterday, it corrects today; its certainties from one era are contradicted by the next.
How can we trust it, then, if it contradicts itself like this?
This common criticism, however, is based on a profound misunderstanding.
For what is presented as a weakness is, in reality, the very strength of science, and what distinguishes it from everything that claims to know without ever questioning itself.
Let’s understand well what 'changing one's mind' means in science.
It does not mean yielding to whim or fashion, but revising one's conclusions in light of new facts.
When an observation contradicts a theory, the scientist does not stubbornly defend their theory against the facts; they modify it or abandon it for a better one.
This ability to correct oneself is not a flaw of scientific knowledge: it is its principle.
Science progresses precisely because it accepts being wrong and rectifying.
What should concern us, then, is not a science that corrects itself, but a knowledge that would never correct itself.
A doctrine that claims to hold a definitive truth, insensitive to any objection or contrary fact, would not be more reliable: it would be dogmatic.

In the face of a complex and partly unknown reality, unwavering certainty is suspect, and the ability to doubt, revise, and admit one’s error is, on the contrary, the mark of an honest relationship with the truth.
Doubt is not the enemy of knowledge; it is its guardian.
It is this methodical doubt that makes science reliable, despite its errors — or rather thanks to its way of dealing with them.
No scientific assertion is safe from being revised one day; all are, by principle, provisional, open to criticism and the test of facts.
This absence of definitive certainty, which may seem a weakness, is what allows science to approach, correction after correction, a progressively more accurate understanding.
What is solid in it is not eternal truths, but a method that learns from its mistakes.
However, one must guard against a misunderstanding.
That science corrects itself does not mean that anything goes, nor that its current conclusions deserve no trust on the grounds that they might change.
A theory that has been thoroughly tested, confirmed by countless observations, deserves our trust, even if the future may refine it.
Because science is revisable, one cannot conclude that its results are without value: that would confuse caution with lazy skepticism.
Doubt, when properly understood, does not weaken science; it is its foundation.
To distrust what never doubts, to trust what accepts correction: this is perhaps the most valuable lesson that science can impart to us, far beyond its results.
For this willingness to revise one’s beliefs in light of the facts is not only a scientific method; it is an intellectual virtue that our debates often sorely lack.

sentences: Every society punishes those who break its most serious rules.
Prison, fines, and various forms of punishment seem obvious, as the idea that a crime should be punished is deeply ingrained in us.
But as soon as we ask why we punish, for what purpose, the answer becomes unclear.
We expect several things from punishment at once, often contradictory, and this confusion of goals explains many of the deadlocks in our penal systems.
A first reason for punishment is to protect society.
By removing someone who has committed a serious act, we prevent them from committing others; the punishment keeps others safe.
This function is real and legitimate: a society has the right to protect itself from those who threaten it.
But it only justifies punishment for as long as the danger persists, and it says nothing about what we owe to someone who is no longer dangerous.
Punishing to protect is a logic of security, not of justice.
A second reason is to deter.
By punishing, we send a warning to everyone: this is what awaits those who transgress.
The fear of punishment would discourage potential criminals.

This deterrent function is often invoked, but its effectiveness is uncertain: the severity of penalties, experience shows, deters less than we think, because those who act rarely believe they will get caught.
And above all, punishing an individual as an example to scare others amounts to treating them as a means, which contradicts the sense of justice.
A third reason, more obscure, is to repay: the guilty must pay, suffer in return for the harm they have done, because it would be just in itself.
This idea, ancient and powerful, responds to a deep feeling — that evil calls for reparation, that impunity is unbearable.
But it is also the closest to revenge, and one might wonder if causing suffering in return adds anything to the world, or merely doubles the evil.
The line between justice that repays and revenge that satisfies is thin.
A fourth reason, finally, is to correct: punishment should aim to amend the guilty, to reintegrate them, to ensure they do not reoffend and find a place in society.
This function, the most future-oriented, is also the most demanding and the most often neglected.
A society that punishes without ever seeking to reintegrate condemns itself to produce recidivists, and fails to provide what it owes even to those who have erred: the possibility of redemption.
These four goals — to protect, to deter, to repay, to correct — coexist in our penal systems without ever fully aligning.
What serves one sometimes undermines the other: the severity that claims to deter or repay often contradicts reintegration.
Reflecting on punishment is primarily about clarifying what we expect from it, and accepting that we cannot achieve everything at once.
A society may be judged less by how it punishes than by the clarity with which it understands why it does so — and by the space it leaves, despite everything, for redemption.

sentences: There is one area where the contrast between the French and the British is always amusing: their relationship with rules.

The British, it is said, respect the rules, queue with exemplary patience, and follow instructions without complaint; the French, on the other hand, discuss the rules, willingly circumvent them, and consider contesting them a right, even a duty.
These images, necessarily simplified, do capture a real difference in how each people relates to authority and norms.
The British respect for rules can be seen in a thousand details of daily life.
The queue, in particular, is a true institution: people spontaneously line up in order, and cutting in line is seen as a serious, almost scandalous offense.
This discipline reflects a deep trust in common rules, regarded as fair and useful, and a strong sense of fair play: everyone plays the game because the game benefits everyone.
Following the rules is not felt as submission, but as a form of civic duty and mutual respect.
The French attitude is more ambivalent.

The French do not despise rules, but they maintain a critical relationship with them: they want to understand their rationale, reserve the right to judge them, and do not hesitate to circumvent them if they find them absurd or unjust.
This disposition has a long history, that of a people who have made contesting authority a driving force in their political history.
Discussing the rules, protesting, and occasionally disobeying are not seen as shameful: it is almost a way to assert one's freedom and critical spirit.
These two attitudes also have their virtues and their downsides.

The British respect for rules produces an orderly, predictable society where communal life unfolds with fluidity and courtesy; however, it can be criticized for a certain docility, a tendency to follow the rules even when they deserve to be contested.

The French critical spirit fosters vigilance towards power, a capacity to revolt against injustice; but it can also lead to indiscipline, systematic contestation, and difficulty in agreeing on common rules.
This contrast points to different conceptions of freedom.
For the British, freedom goes well with respecting rules, provided they are just and accepted: obeying a rule one approves of does not alienate in any way.
For the French, freedom implies the permanent right to judge the rule, to contest it, and not to submit to it blindly: obedience without examination seems suspicious to them.
One sees in the rule a pact that protects everyone's freedom; the other sees it as a power that must always be treated with caution.
None of these attitudes is superior in itself.
A society undoubtedly needs both: the respect for rules that allows for living together, and the critical spirit that prevents unjust rules from persisting.
The British could sometimes benefit from contesting more; the French could benefit from respecting more.
By observing each other, everyone can see what is excessive in their own relationship with rules — and what they could borrow from their neighbor.

sentences: The idea of progress is so deeply ingrained in us that we take it for granted.
We spontaneously believe that history is moving forward, that humanity, despite setbacks, is improving, and that tomorrow will be better than yesterday.
This belief shapes our relationship with time, justifies our efforts, and comforts us in our sorrows.
However, it is relatively recent in the grand scheme of history and far from being self-evident.
Questioning it is not falling into pessimism, but examining one of the most powerful assumptions of our civilization.
The idea of progress has considerable merits to defend.

In many respects, the improvement is undeniable: life expectancy has increased, physical suffering has decreased, diseases have been conquered, education has spread, and forms of cruelty that were once commonplace have become intolerable.
Anyone who would deny these advances, in the name of a nostalgia for an idealized past, would be gravely mistaken and would insult those who, in the past, died young, in pain and ignorance.
There is indeed progress, and failing to recognize it would be both a mistake and an ingratitude.
But the idea of progress, as soon as it becomes doctrine, carries illusions that must be uncovered.
The first is to believe that progress is necessary, inscribed in the very meaning of history, as if a force guaranteed it.
Nothing could be further from the truth.
Nothing assures that what has been gained cannot be lost; history knows regressions, collapses, and returns of barbarism that were thought to be behind us.
Progress, when it occurs, is the result of efforts and choices, not a law of history; to take it for granted is to stop defending it, and thus prepare for its loss.
The second illusion is to believe in unified progress, as if improvement affects all areas at once.
However, one can progress in one area and regress in another.
Technical power is increasing, but is our wisdom keeping pace?
We treat better, but we destroy our environment; we communicate more, but we may understand each other less; we know more, but do we know how to live better?
Material and technical progress, undeniable, does not guarantee moral or human progress, and it can even, by increasing our powers without increasing our wisdom, make our faults more perilous.
Confusing the different types of progress is merely self-deception.
The third illusion, more subtle, concerns the measurement of progress.
Progress towards what?
Saying that history is improving implies a criterion, an idea of what is better.
However, this criterion is not given; it depends on what we value.
A civilization that judges progress by power and wealth does not measure the same thing as one that would judge it by justice or quality of life.
The idea of progress often conceals this assumption: it presents as an objective advance what is merely a movement towards what we consider desirable.
Questioning progress means questioning our own values, which we project onto history while believing we can read a meaning that it contains.
Should we therefore abandon the idea of progress?
That would mean giving up what gives human action part of its drive: the hope of making the world better.

But we must hold it differently: not as a law of history that carries us along, but as a task that is our responsibility; not as an established fact, but as a fragile possibility; not as a unified and guaranteed movement, but as an effort that is always partial, reversible, and to be resumed.
A progress understood this way is more modest, but more true, and above all more demanding: it does not exempt us from acting, it obliges us to do so.
For if nothing guarantees that tomorrow will be better, then it depends on us to make it so.

sentences: At the end of this journey between France and Great Britain, a conclusion emerges that goes beyond simple comparison.
These two neighbors, who have so much that divides and unites them, are not just figures of an old rivalry; they are, for each other, a mirror and a lesson.
For each holds, in its temperament and values, a part of what the other lacks, and their very difference, which is the source of so many misunderstandings, is also an invitation to learn.
Understanding what each people can learn from the other means making comparison not a ranking, but a reflection on what, in each culture, deserves to be complemented.
What could the French sensibility learn from the British sensibility?
First, perhaps, a sense of pragmatism, this distrust of grand abstract principles pushed to their consequences without regard for reality.
The French taste for the universal and the systematic, so fruitful, could sometimes benefit from being more grounded in experience, being wary of logics that, taken to extremes, ignore realities.

It could also learn the respect for rules and fair play, this civic trust that facilitates the smoothness of communal life, where the dissenting spirit, as precious as it may be, sometimes leads to sterile indiscipline.
Finally, it could learn a certain reserve, an art of understatement, a modesty that tempers enthusiasm.
What could the British sensibility learn from the French sensibility?

Perhaps the courage of principles, this ability to rise above the particular case to establish universal values by which to judge and act; pragmatism, as wise as it may be, sometimes lacks the compass that principles provide.

It could learn the art of living, this refusal to subordinate all pleasure to utility, this legitimacy granted to enjoyment, slowness, and conviviality, where a certain austerity has long regarded these pleasures as suspect.
It could also learn a certain intellectual boldness, this taste for thought that dares to tackle big questions and systems, where empiricism sometimes settles for the concrete.
This reciprocity of lessons reveals that the virtues of each people are also its limits, and that its limits are the virtues of the other.
British pragmatism is a strength that becomes a weakness when it lacks principles; French universalism is a strength that becomes a weakness when it loses touch with reality.
British respect for rules is a strength that can turn into docility; the French critical spirit is a strength that can turn into anarchy.
Each quality contains its flaw, and the flaw of one often corresponds to the quality of the other.
That is why they can, by observing each other, learn from one another what they lack.
This lesson extends beyond the case of France and Great Britain.

It illustrates what a fruitful relationship to cultural otherness can be: not the contempt of one who judges the other from their own values, nor the blind admiration that would renounce one’s own, but the mutual learning of one who recognizes in the other a part of what they lack.
Each culture, having developed certain virtues at the cost of others, can find in its neighbors what it has neglected.
The difference between peoples, a source of so many conflicts, is also a wealth, provided it is experienced as an opportunity to learn rather than as a rivalry to win.

Thus, the old rivalry between France and Great Britain, marked by wars, mockery, and mutual fascination, can transform into something else: a conversation where each, in the mirror of the other, learns to know themselves better and to complement one another.
Neither has the right against the other; each is right in their own way, and wrong in their own way, and it is from their very difference that they can benefit.

For those learning a language, and through it a culture, this may be the most beautiful lesson: that the foreigner is not a rival to be defeated nor a model to be imitated, but a possible other self, who reveals to us what we are and invites us to become more.

sentences: We lament forgetting as a failure, a weakness of memory, a loss.
We want to remember everything, to let nothing slip away, and sometimes we envy those whose memory seems infallible.
However, this aspiration for total memory is based on a profound misunderstanding.
For a perfect memory, one that would lose nothing and retain everything with equal clarity, would not be a blessing, but a curse.
Forgetting is not only the enemy of memory; it is its necessary condition, and more broadly, the condition of life, thought, and action.
We must rehabilitate forgetting, not as a lesser evil, but as a grace.
Let’s imagine what existence would be like without forgetting.

The one who would remember everything, absolutely everything, with the same intensity — every detail of every day, every perception, every word heard — would be overwhelmed by the weight of their memory.
Unable to distinguish the important from the insignificant, since everything would be equally present, they would be unable to think, act, or live.

For thinking requires abstraction, generalization, and neglecting details to grasp the essential; acting requires focusing on what matters now, while setting aside the rest; living requires letting the past pass, not being glued to every moment that has gone by.
A total memory would make all of this impossible; it would trap one in a perpetually cluttered present filled with all the past, unable to sort, prioritize, or forget what needs to be forgotten.
A perfect memory would be a prison.
Forgetting, far from being a failure, is therefore an essential function, as necessary as memory itself.
It sorts, it lightens, it erases the insignificant to let the important stand out; it frees us from the burden of an entire past, allowing us to concentrate, generalize, and think.

Without forgetting, there is no abstraction, for to abstract is to forget particulars; no concentration, for to concentrate is to forget everything else; no life directed towards the future, for living is to let the past fade away.
Forgetting is not the opposite of memory, but its necessary complement, what makes it livable and fruitful.
A memory that would not forget would not be a superior memory; it would be a monstrous memory, incapable of serving life.
Forgetting is also the condition of happiness, or at least of serenity.
For we must forget not only the insignificant but also part of our pains, offenses, and failures, in order to continue living.
The one who would forget none of their sufferings, no wounds, no humiliations, who would keep them all alive and present, would be overwhelmed, unable to heal, forgive, or turn towards the future.
Forgetting is what heals, what allows time to do its work of soothing, what frees us from the rumination of past ills.
We need to forget in order not to be crushed by the weight of all we have suffered; forgetting is a grace that makes life possible.
There is something even deeper.
Forgetting is linked to our capacity to change, to become others, to free ourselves from what we were.

A memory that would retain everything would chain us to our past, to our mistakes, to what we have been; forgetting, by allowing part of that past to fade, enables us not to be prisoners of it, to transform ourselves, to start anew.
It is what makes forgiveness possible — both of others and of oneself — second chances, renewal.
A being without forgetting would be frozen in their entire past, unable to become anything other than what their total memory would have fixed.
Forgetting is thus linked to freedom itself, to the possibility of not being absolutely determined by everything that has been.
Rehabilitating forgetting is therefore not praising negligence or amnesia, nor denying the value of memory, which remains essential.
It is recognizing that forgetting and memory are two sides of the same faculty, equally necessary, and that the aspiration for total memory misunderstands the vital function of forgetting.
We need to remember, but also to forget; to retain the essential, but to let the rest fade; to keep alive what must be, but to let time soothe what needs to be.
Wisdom regarding time and memory consists not in retaining everything, but in forgetting well — in letting go of what must pass, to keep alive and free the memory of what matters.
For it is also through what one consents to forget that a being remains capable of living, thinking, and becoming.

sentences: When individuals gather in a crowd, a transformation occurs that has always fascinated and worried observers of social life.

The individual, caught up in the crowd, seems to become someone else: they are swept away by collective emotions, act in ways they would disapprove of alone, and lose part of their judgment, responsibility, and even individuality.

This phenomenon, where numbers transform beings and the individual dissolves into the collective, touches on deep springs of social life, and understanding it is necessary to consider both the dangers and the possibilities of human gathering.
What first strikes one about crowd behavior is the way they often lower the level of awareness and responsibility of the individuals that make them up.

In the crowd, the individual feels anonymous, diluted, relieved of the responsibility that weighs on them when acting alone; they are swept up by collective emotions that spread from person to person, amplified by numbers; they lose their critical sense, restraint, and the judgment that usually governs them.
The crowd can thus lead individuals to acts that none would commit alone, to violence, cruelty, and frenzies that each, once again an individual, would be astonished and frightened by.
The number seems to free what individual consciousness contained, dissolve inhibitions, and lower the being to the level of a collective emotion that surpasses it.
This dark side of crowds has fueled a long tradition of distrust towards them, which sees gathering as a regression, a dissolution of the civilized individual into an irrational and dangerous mass.
This distrust is not unfounded: history is full of examples of crowds gone mad, swept away by hatred, fear, and exaltation, capable of the worst atrocities.
Power, moreover, knows how to exploit this transformation, manipulate crowds, incite collective frenzies that serve its ends, and dissolve critical individuals into a docile or fanatic mass.
The crowd is a formidable instrument, and its ability to abolish individual judgment makes it a danger to reason and freedom.
But it would be one-sided to see only this troubling face of crowds.
For the gathering of individuals is not always a regression; it can also be an elevation, strength, and solidarity.

Crowds are not only capable of the worst; they are also capable of the best, of the collective drive towards justice, of the solidarity that unites, of the courage that numbers give to those who would not dare alone.

The great movements of emancipation, the resistances to oppression, the bursts of collective generosity, are also crowd phenomena, where numbers, far from lowering, elevate, where gathering provides the strength of what no isolated individual could achieve.
The crowd that rises against injustice, that finds in numbers the courage to resist, manifests another face of gathering, no less real than its dark side.
How can we understand this ambivalence?
Perhaps by recognizing that the crowd amplifies, rather than creates, that it multiplies the possibilities contained within individuals, for better or for worse.

The number dissolves individual responsibility, but this dissolution can free both violence and courage, cruelty and generosity; it spreads emotions, but these emotions can be hatred as well as enthusiasm for a just cause.
What determines the face that a crowd takes on are the representations that run through it, the narratives that animate it, the ends towards which it is directed.
The same force of numbers can serve oppression or emancipation, depending on what moves it.
The crowd is neither good nor bad in itself; it is an ambivalent power, whose orientation determines its value.

Understanding the crowd and the individual, therefore, means escaping two one-sided visions: the one that sees in crowds only danger and regression, leading to an aristocratic distrust of any popular gathering; and the one that idealizes them, seeing in the gathered people an infallible innocence and wisdom.
The truth is that the gathering of individuals is an ambivalent power, capable of the worst and the best, and vigilance consists in knowing its springs so as not to be its plaything.

Knowing how numbers transform us, how they can lower our judgment or elevate our courage, how they can be manipulated or lead to emancipation, is to give ourselves the means to participate in crowds without dissolving into them, to bring the best rather than the worst, and to remain a conscious individual within the gathering.
For the challenge is not to flee from crowds, without which nothing collective is achieved, but to remain oneself, clear-sighted and responsible, amidst the ambivalent power of numbers.

sentences: This year, I fulfilled a dream: to run a full marathon, forty-two kilometers.
Two years earlier, I couldn't even run five minutes without stopping.
The journey has been long.
To prepare myself, I trained for six months, with a very precise plan.
I ran four times a week, sometimes even in the rain.
On the day of the marathon, more than ten thousand runners gathered in the streets of the city.
The first twenty kilometers went well.
I felt strong, almost light.
Then, around the thirtieth kilometer, everything changed.
My legs became very heavy.
They call it 'the wall,' and I understand why now.
I wanted to give up.
But I thought about all those months of training, about all those tough hours.
So I slowed down, but I didn't stop.
Kilometer after kilometer, I kept going.
The last five kilometers were the longest of my life.
When I finally crossed the finish line, after four hours and twenty minutes, I cried from exhaustion and pride.
I may never do another marathon.
But I am happy to know that I finished one.

Don't worry, she reassured me.
These things happen; people generally understand.

sentences: While looking at my listening history from the past few months, I noticed something strange.
During a stressful period at work in February, I had listened almost exclusively to very calm, almost meditative music.
I hadn't realized it at the time.
Then, in spring, when everything was better, my listening had become much more energetic, with fast rhythms and optimistic lyrics.
By observing this evolution, I understood that my music acted like a sort of diary, without me having consciously decided it.
A psychologist friend, to whom I shared this discovery, explained to me that this phenomenon is well documented.
The music we choose often reflects our emotional state, sometimes even before we are fully aware of it ourselves.
This idea made me think differently about my own listening habits.
Maybe I should pay more attention to what I choose to listen to, not just as entertainment, but as a subtle indicator of my own inner state.
A friend, to whom I shared this discovery, checked her own history and found exactly the same pattern: softer music during her difficult times, more upbeat as soon as everything got better.
Since then, we joke half-seriously from time to time about how our current playlist is doing.
Today, when I notice that I'm returning to particularly melancholic music for several days in a row, I ask myself: what in my life right now might deserve a little more attention?
Music, often without us realizing it, may say more about us than our own words.

sentences: The day my company told me that I could work from home, I felt a real sense of relief.
No more daily commute, no more waking up at six o'clock, no more noisy office.
On the first morning, I enjoyed this change: a quiet breakfast, coffee on my makeshift terrace on the balcony, and then opening my computer at exactly nine o'clock.
However, I quickly discovered difficulties that I hadn't anticipated.
Without colleagues around me, some simple questions took much longer to resolve, through written messages rather than by turning to someone.
Around eleven o'clock, I realized that I hadn't spoken to anyone in person since the night before.
This silence, which I imagined would be restful, felt strangely heavy.
I also noticed that I was working, without realizing it, much later than usual.
Without the ritual of leaving the office, it was hard to know when to really stop.

The following days taught me that I needed to relearn how to structure my own day, without the markers that the office used to provide: the collective lunch break, the back-and-forth between meetings, the little interruptions that naturally punctuated time.
All of this had to be recreated voluntarily, without any external pressure pushing me to do so.
My first day didn't go as I had imagined: neither the dreamed freedom nor the disaster feared by some.
Just a new way of working, with its own rules to create.

sentences: The village where my grandparents grew up had more than a thousand inhabitants fifty years ago.
Today, barely two hundred people still live there year-round.
Agriculture, which was once the main activity of the village, has gradually disappeared, pushing many residents to leave in search of work elsewhere, in the big cities.
What has allowed the village to not completely disappear is paradoxically tourism, developed thanks to an old medieval castle located on the heights.

For about fifteen years, this castle has attracted thousands of visitors every summer, which has led to the opening of several businesses: a restaurant, two hotels, and a small shop selling local products.
My grandmother, who has long regretted the decline of her hometown, acknowledges that this tourism has indirectly given her a form of life she thought was lost.
"It's not the same village as before, she often tells me, but at least it still exists."
During my last visit, I met several young people who returned to settle in the village, drawn by these jobs related to tourism, after having left for the city to find work a few years earlier.
This modest return gives the village a younger population than it has known for decades.

This story illustrates a complex reality well: tourism, often criticized for its negative effects on certain places, can also represent a real economic lifeline for other places threatened with disappearance.

sentences: One day, I calculated the number of plastic bottles I bought each year, almost out of curiosity.
The result surprised me: about three bottles a day, which added up to more than a thousand bottles a year, just for me.
This figure, once written down, seemed hard to ignore.
I decided to invest in a reusable water bottle, determined to change this habit that had been ingrained for years.
The change, however, didn't happen as easily as I had imagined.
Used to buying a bottle whenever I was thirsty, whether out, at work, or in the car, I often forgot to fill my bottle in advance.
In the first few weeks, I found myself without water several times, forced to buy a plastic bottle again, a bit disappointed in my lack of consistency.
Gradually, I developed new habits: systematically filling my bottle before going out, always keeping one in my bag and another in my car.
Today, almost a year after this decision, I estimate that I have reduced my consumption of plastic bottles by more than ninety percent.

Counting, week after week, the number of bottles I no longer buy brings a nearly accounting-like satisfaction: a concrete figure that makes visible a change that would otherwise have remained abstract and easy to forget in the whirlwind of daily life.
This change, which seemed simple on paper, reminded me that an old habit takes time and patience to truly transform.

sentences: An entire generation has now grown up spending a significant part of its childhood and adolescence in virtual worlds that exist only in digital form, a formative experience radically different from that of all previous generations.

This reality raises unprecedented questions, still largely unexplored by research: what effect does forming some of one's first friendships, experiencing some of one's first strong emotions, or building part of one's personal identity within entirely virtual environments rather than physical ones have on an individual's psychological and social development?

Some researchers in developmental psychology highlight legitimate concerns: virtual interactions, no matter how rich, could deprive young people of certain fundamental social learnings, normally acquired through physical presence and the subtle body signals of face-to-face interaction.

Other researchers take a more nuanced perspective, reminding us that every generation has always had to adapt to new technological environments, without this necessarily meaning a degradation of fundamental relational abilities, but rather the development of social skills suited to these new contexts, different but not necessarily inferior to those of previous generations.

It is probably too early to definitively settle this debate, as the first generations that have grown up almost entirely immersed in these digital worlds have not yet reached an age sufficient to allow for a complete and rigorous evaluation of the long-term effects of this unprecedented formative experience in human history, of which we may still only measure a fraction of the real consequences.

sentences: The public space, as envisioned by the theorists of modern democracy, was supposed to be a common ground where citizens, informed by the same sources, could confront their opinions against a shared backdrop of facts and references.

Social networks, by promising to democratize speech by making it accessible to everyone, have paradoxically accelerated the erosion of this common ground, replacing the relative unity of the past with a multiplication of largely impermeable digital bubbles.

This fragmentation does not result from a deliberate intention to divide, but from a technical logic that appears almost innocuous: the algorithms that organize our news feeds are designed to maximize engagement, and nothing engages a user more than content that confirms what they already believe.

As a result, there is a continuous, invisible, and cumulative selection that exposes each person to an informational reality that increasingly aligns with their pre-existing preferences and becomes increasingly foreign to what others perceive.

The outcome of this process is not just an increased disagreement over opinions, which would be somewhat trivial and even healthy in a vibrant democracy, but an increasingly radical disagreement over the facts themselves.

Two citizens, exposed to sufficiently divergent informational environments, no longer discuss the same events interpreted differently; they literally inhabit distinct realities, built on sources, narratives, and sometimes contradictory facts.

However, a debate requires common ground: without it, the exchange degenerates into a dialogue of the deaf, where each person speaks from their own world without ever truly encountering that of the other.
Some will object that this fragmentation is nothing new, that societies have always experienced divisions of opinion, partisan newspapers, and closed circles.

This reservation is not unfounded, but it overlooks a difference in degree that becomes, at a certain threshold, a difference in nature: never before has the personalization of information reached such fine granularity, nor operated on such a massive scale, simultaneously affecting billions of individuals according to criteria optimized in real time by systems whose logic largely escapes the understanding, and even the control, of their own designers.
However, it would be excessive to attribute the entire responsibility for this fragmentation solely to algorithms.

After all, they exploit pre-existing and deeply human cognitive tendencies: the preference for what reassures us, the instinctive distrust of what contradicts us, the pleasure of belonging to a homogeneous thought community.
Social networks did not invent these trends; they have multiplied and industrialized them, providing an unprecedented scale and efficiency of expression.
Some researchers have indeed attempted to quantify this fragmentation by measuring the actual overlap of information sources consulted by politically opposing groups within the same society.

The results, consistent from one study to another, show a progressively reduced overlap over the years, empirically corroborating what daily observation had already suggested: two citizens from the same country, sometimes from the same city, end up getting their information from sources that are almost entirely disconnected, with not a single common informational point on which to base a genuine dialogue.
In light of this observation, the proposed remedies remain of uncertain scope.
Regulating algorithms, demanding greater transparency, encouraging a wider diversity of exposure: these avenues, while not without merit, face a deeper, almost anthropological obstacle.

For it is not enough to modify technical tools to restore a unified public space; it is also necessary to convince individuals, who are structurally inclined to prefer the comfort of confirmation over the discomfort of contradiction, to actively seek out what disturbs them.

This requirement, which assumes a rare intellectual discipline, cannot be decreed solely through software engineering; it pertains to a culture that must be patiently cultivated against the natural inclination of our minds.

Among the cartilaginous fish: petromyzon-prickas, a type of eel, fifteen inches long, with a greenish head, purple fins, a bluish-gray back, a brownish-silver belly sprinkled with bright spots, and golden-ringed irises; curious creatures that the current of the Amazon must have carried out to sea, as they inhabit freshwater; tuberculated rays with pointed snouts, long and slender tails, armed with a long serrated spine; small sharks about a meter long, grayish and whitish in color, whose teeth, arranged in several rows, curve backward, commonly known as pantouffliers; lophies-vespertillions, a type of reddish isosceles triangle half a meter long, whose pectoral fins are connected by fleshy extensions that give them the appearance of bats, but which have been nicknamed sea unicorns due to their bony appendage near the nostrils; finally, a few species of batistes, the curassavian with dotted sides shining in a brilliant golden color, and the light violet caprisque, with iridescent hues like a pigeon's throat.

sentences: Meanwhile, time was passing; night fell; the sounds of the street quieted down; my uncle, still bent over his work, saw nothing, not even the maid Marthe who slightly opened the door; he heard nothing, not even the voice of that worthy servant, saying:
“Will sir have dinner this evening?”

So Marthe had to leave without an answer: as for me, after resisting for a while, I was overcome by an irresistible sleep, and I fell asleep on a corner of the sofa, while my uncle Lidenbrock continued to calculate and cross out.
When I woke up the next day, the tireless digger was still at work.

His red eyes, pale complexion, tangled hair under his feverish hand, and flushed cheeks clearly indicated his terrible struggle with the impossible, and what mental fatigue, what strain on his brain, the hours must have been for him.
Truly, he inspired pity in me.
Despite the reproaches I believed I had the right to make, a certain emotion overcame me.

The poor man was so possessed by his idea that he forgot to get angry; all his vital forces were concentrated on a single point, and since they were not escaping through their usual outlet, one could fear that their tension would make him explode at any moment.
I could have loosened that iron vise that was tightening around his head with just a gesture, with just a word!
And I did nothing.
However, I had a good heart.
Why did I remain silent in such a situation?
In the very interest of my uncle.
"No, no, I repeated, no, I will not speak!"
He would want to go there, I know him; nothing would stop him.
It's a volcanic imagination, and to do what other geologists haven't done, he would risk his life.
I will remain silent; I will keep this secret that chance has made me master of; to reveal it would be to kill Professor Lidenbrock.
Let him guess it, if he can; I don't want to blame myself one day for leading him to his doom.

sentences: The supper was quickly devoured, and the little group settled in as best they could.
The bedding was hard, the shelter flimsy, and the situation quite uncomfortable, five thousand feet above sea level.
However, my sleep was particularly peaceful that night, one of the best I had had in a long time.
I didn't even dream.
The next day, we woke up half-frozen by the brisk air, under the rays of a beautiful sun.
I got out of my granite bed and went to enjoy the magnificent sight that was unfolding before me.
I was at the summit of one of the two peaks of Sneffels, the southern one.
From there, my view extended over most of the island; the optics, common to all great heights, highlighted the shores, while the central parts seemed to sink.

It looked as if one of those relief maps by Helbesmer was spread out beneath my feet; I could see the deep valleys crossing in all directions, the cliffs digging in like wells, the lakes turning into ponds, and the rivers becoming streams.
To my right, countless glaciers and numerous peaks succeeded one another, some of which were crowned with light smoke.
The undulations of these infinite mountains, which their layers of snow seemed to make frothy, reminded me of the surface of a choppy sea.
If I turned to the west, the Ocean unfolded there in its majestic expanse, like a continuation of those fluffy summits.
Where the land ended and where the waves began, my eye could barely distinguish it.
I thus immersed myself in that prestigious ecstasy that high peaks provide, and this time, without vertigo, for I was finally getting used to these sublime contemplations.

My dazzled gaze bathed in the transparent irradiation of the sun's rays; I forgot who I was, where I was, to live the life of elves or sylphs, imaginary inhabitants of Scandinavian mythology; I was intoxicated by the pleasure of the heights, without thinking of the abysses into which my fate was soon to plunge me.
But I was brought back to the feeling of reality by the arrival of the professor and Hans, who joined me at the summit of the peak.
My uncle, turning to the west, pointed out to me with his hand a slight vapor, a mist, an appearance of land that dominated the line of the waves.

sentences: It was November 22.
The final departure was scheduled to take place ten days later.
Only one operation remained to be successfully completed, a delicate and perilous task that required infinite precautions, and against the success of which Captain Nicholl had wagered his third bet.
It was, in fact, about loading the Columbiad and introducing the four hundred thousand pounds of fulmi-cotton into it.

Nicholl had thought, perhaps not without reason, that handling such a formidable quantity of pyroxyl would lead to serious catastrophes, and that in any case this highly explosive mass would ignite by itself under the pressure of the projectile.
There were serious dangers further increased by the carelessness and lightheartedness of the Americans, who had no qualms about loading their bombs with a cigar in their mouths during the Civil War.

But Barbicane was determined to succeed and not to fail at the port; he therefore chose his best workers, had them operate under his watchful eye, did not take his eyes off them for a moment, and, through carefulness and precautions, he managed to stack all the odds in his favor for success.
First of all, he made sure not to bring all his cargo to the enclosure of Stone's Hill.
He had it brought in gradually in perfectly sealed containers.

The four hundred thousand pounds of pyroxyl had been divided into packages of five hundred pounds, resulting in eight hundred large cartridges carefully made by the most skilled artificers in Pensacola.
Each container could hold ten and arrived one after the other via the Tampa-Town railroad; this way, there were never more than five thousand pounds of pyroxyl in the enclosure at any one time.
As soon as it arrived, each container was unloaded by barefoot workers, and each cartridge was transported to the opening of the Columbiad, where it was lowered using cranes operated by hand.
All steam machines had been removed, and even the smallest fires were extinguished within a two-mile radius.
It was already too much to have to protect these masses of fulmi-cotton from the heat of the sun, even in November.
Thus, work was preferably done at night, under the glow of a light produced in a vacuum that, using Ruhmkorff's devices, created artificial daylight all the way to the bottom of the Columbiad.
There, the cartridges were arranged with perfect regularity and connected to each other by a metal wire intended to simultaneously carry the electric spark to the center of each one.

They spoke of a river by which Lake Ukéréoué drains to the north, and that river exists, and we are going down it, and it flows with a speed comparable to our own!

sentences: The day of May 17 was calm and free of any incident; the desert was beginning again; a moderate wind was carrying the Victoria southwest; it did not deviate to the right or to the left; its shadow traced a perfectly straight line on the sand.
Before his departure, the doctor had cautiously replenished his water supply; he feared he might not be able to land in these regions infested by the Aouelimminien Tuareg.
The plateau, elevated eighteen hundred feet above sea level, sloped downwards towards the south.

The travelers, having crossed the frequently trodden route from Aghadès to Mourzouk, arrived in the evening at 16° latitude and 4° 55' longitude, after covering one hundred eighty miles of long monotony.
During this day, Joe prepared the last pieces of game, which had only received a cursory preparation; he served very appetizing snipe skewers for dinner.
The wind being favorable, the doctor decided to continue his journey during a night that the moon, almost full still, made radiant.
The Victoria ascended to a height of five hundred feet, and during this nighttime crossing of about sixty miles, even a light child's sleep would not have been disturbed.

sentences: In my day, we would stand up when an adult entered; we would say hello, ma'am; we didn't interrupt.
How many times have you heard this refrain?
It has crossed the centuries, remarkably stable.
Socrates, too, would have complained about the insolent youth of his time.
Each generation, upon reaching a certain age, looks at the next one and diagnoses the same fatal disease: the end of politeness.
The fact that this complaint has been repeated identically for two thousand five hundred years should make us sit up and take notice.
If politeness really disappeared with each generation, there would have been nothing left of it long ago.
Yet it is still here.
So it doesn't die; it just shifts.
For we must distinguish between two things that nostalgia confuses: the forms of politeness and its principle.
The forms, yes, change, and sometimes quickly.

Removing one's hat in front of a lady, kissing the hand, using formal phrases: these gestures, once mandatory, have largely disappeared, and anyone who would practice them today would seem affected rather than courteous.
Similarly, the use of 'tu' has gained ground, dress codes have relaxed, and deference towards age and rank has diminished.
Seen through these old forms, yes, the world seems impolite.
But let's look at what has replaced them, for the space has never remained empty.
Our time has invented its own demands, often more subtle and sometimes heavier than the old ones.

Today, we pay much more attention than before to not hurting anyone with our words; words that were once commonplace have become unacceptable, because we take into account people whom the old politeness superbly ignored.
We apologize for disturbing, we thank in writing, we ask for permission to photograph someone.
Politeness towards women has changed in nature: fewer hands kissed, more real respect.
What we have lost in ceremony, we may have regained in consideration.
It is not about denying any problem.

Traffic, the anonymity of cities, and the brutality of certain online exchanges create very real forms of rudeness, and the screen, which puts a face at a distance, disinhibits rudeness that one wouldn't dare express face to face.
Every era has its areas of harshness.
But the idea of a general collapse does not hold up to scrutiny: it stems from that persistent illusion that beautifies the past and darkens the present.
What remains, beneath the changing forms, is the principle: this movement by which I recognize the other, I take their existence into account, I show them that they matter.
This principle, in fact, does not date from any era and does not belong to any.
It is the discreet cement of all communal life.
Our grandchildren, one day, will judge our manners outdated and will mourn the politeness of 'their time' — that is to say, ours.
They will be wrong, just like us.
And politeness, for its part, will continue on its way.

We say the opposite of what we think, with a serious face, and the other person has to understand.

And Mathieu appeared in the doorway.
He was a sixty-year-old man, thin, with a goatee and long white mustaches.
My companion shook his hand, introduced me, and Mathieu let us into a cool kitchen that also served as his dining room.
He said:
"Well, sir, I don't have a fancy apartment.
I really like not to stray far from the food.
The pots and pans, you see, they provide company."
Then, turning to my friend:
"Why are you coming on a Thursday?
You know it's my Boss's consultation day.
I can't go out this afternoon."
And, running to the door, he let out a terrifying bellow: "Mélie-e-e!" which must have made the sailors on the ships going up or down the river, way down in the hollow valley, look up.
Mélie did not reply.
Then Mathieu winked mischievously.
--"She's not happy with me, you see, because yesterday I found myself in the ninety."
My neighbor started to laugh: --"In the ninety, Mathieu!
How did you manage that?"
Mathieu replied:
I'll tell you.
Last year, I only found twenty bushels of apricot apples.
There aren't any left; but for making cider, that's all there is.
So I made a batch that I tapped yesterday.
For nectar, it's nectar; you'll hear about it.
I had Polyte here; we started having a drink, and then another, without getting enough (we could drink until tomorrow), so that, from drink to drink, I feel a freshness in my stomach.
I said to Polyte, "How about we have a glass of fine to warm up?"
He agreed.
But that fine, it sets your body on fire, so we had to go back to the cider.
But then, from freshness to warmth and from warmth to freshness, I realize that I'm at ninety.
